6	## Bubble Tea Application Structure
7	
8	This is a **multi-view TUI application** using the Elm Architecture (TEA) pattern via Bubble Tea. Understanding the routing and view lifecycle is critical:
9	
10	**Main Components:**
11	- `main.go` - Entry point, initializes config and Bubble Tea program
12	- `internal/app/app.go` - **Router/orchestrator** that manages view switching and command mode
13	- `internal/app/messages.go` - Cross-view messages (GitLab, scan results, pull, etc.)
14	- `internal/shared/state.go` - SharedState for cross-view data (GitLab client, user, stats)
15	- `internal/ui/*/` - Individual views
16	
17	**Key Architecture Pattern:**
18	```
19	App (Router)
20	├── Manages: currentView, commandMode, viewport, sharedState
21	├── Routes messages to active view
22	├── Handles view switching via command parser
23	├── Manages multi-context configuration
24	└── Views (lazy-loaded):
25	    ├── dashboard       - Overview (stats, tools, service status)
26	    ├── status          - System monitoring (CRUD monitors)
27	    ├── git-auth        - forge authentication form (GitLab or GitHub)
28	    ├── git-explorer    - forge namespace/repository browser + multi-select clone
29	    ├── workspaces      - Local workspace management + git metadata
30	    ├── security        - Trivy + Gitleaks scanner with multi-tab results
31	    ├── containers      - Docker container list + live metrics
32	    ├── oci-resources   - OCI resource list, scan, launch containers, network inspection
33	    ├── netdiag         - Network diagnostics (Docker-based tools) + real-time port monitor
34	    ├── configuration   - Every scalar setting in the current context
35	    ├── jobs            - Long-running work: runs, then their targets
36	    ├── templates       - Catalog of repository templates: git, local or OCI sources
37	    ├── files           - Whole-filesystem browser, and the path picker forms borrow
38	    ├── about           - Which build is running, and where it keeps its files
39	    └── viewer          - One document, read-only (router-only: no `:viewer`)
40	```
41	
42	## View Switching & Command Mode
43	
44	Press `ctrl+p` to enter command mode, then type:
45	- `dashboard` or `d` - Switch to dashboard view
46	- `status` or `s` - Switch to status view
47	- `git-auth` or `ga` - Switch to the forge authentication view
48	- `git-explorer` or `ge` - Switch to the forge explorer view
49	- `workspaces` or `w` - Switch to workspaces view
50	- `security` or `sec` - Switch to security scanner view
51	- `containers`, `cont` or `ct` - Switch to containers view
52	- `oci-resources` or `oci` - Switch to OCI resources view
53	- `netdiag` or `net` - Switch to network diagnostics view
54	- `configuration`, `config` or `cfg` - Switch to the configuration view
55	- `jobs` or `j` - Switch to the jobs view: what is running, and what ran this session
56	- `templates` or `tpl` - Switch to the repository template catalog (see [templates.md](templates.md))
57	- `files` or `fs` - Browse the whole filesystem: create and delete files and directories; also the picker a form's path field opens with enter (see [filebrowser.md](filebrowser.md))
58	- `about` or `version` - Which build is running: version, commit, build date, and where the config, cache and log live
59	- `context <name>` or `ctx <name>` - Switch configuration context
60	- `context list` - Show available contexts
61	- `quit` - Exit application
62	
63	In command mode, `tab` swaps the command line for a circular breadcrumb of every view by full name (`command.ViewNames()`): ←/→ (or `tab`) move, `enter` opens, `esc` returns to the command line with its text kept. State is `App.viewPicker*`; rendering is `renderViewPicker` in `app_header.go`.
64	
65	Command parsing and tab-completion live in `internal/command/`. `ParseCommand()` returns a structured `Command{Type, View, Args}` supporting `CommandView`, `CommandContext`, `CommandQuit`, `CommandUnknown`.
66	
67	**The forge views are `git-auth` and `git-explorer`, named after the role.**
68	A context targets one forge (§3.6), so there is one authentication screen and
69	one explorer, and both adapt to whichever it is — a `gitlab-` prefix would have
70	to be typed as `github-` half the time for the same view. Their packages live
71	under `internal/ui/forge/`, which is what the import line says too.
72	
73	**The ten forge-prefixed spellings — `gitlab-auth`, `gla`, `github-auth`, `gha`
74	and their explorer counterparts, plus the older `explorer` / `exp` — no longer
75	parse at all.** They lived in a `legacyNames` table for a transition period
76	after §3.6 renamed the views, resolving without being suggested so muscle
77	memory would not break outright. That table has been removed: one spelling per
78	view, no exceptions, and `git-auth`/`ga`, `git-explorer`/`ge` are the only ones
79	a client gets.
80	
81	**There is no `:theme` command.** The theme is a setting, so the configuration
82	view owns it — the picker wrote `app.theme` behind the settings form's back,
83	which is one setting with two writers. Its overlay, `internal/app/theme.go` and
84	`CommandTheme` are all gone; `applyThemeNow` in `internal/app/configuration.go`
85	is what swaps the palette now.
86	
87	**`ctrl+p` is the way in, and `:` is the convenience.** `ctrl+p` is handled
88	before any `InEditMode()` check, so no text field can claim it; a bare `:` opens
89	the command line too, but only when nothing is focused — inside a field it is an
90	ordinary character, which a value like `https://trivy-server:4954` needs.
91	
92	It is not `ctrl+:` — `:` is 0x3A, outside the 0x40-0x5F range a terminal
93	encodes for Ctrl, so that combination never arrives. It was `alt+:` until
94	§3.26, which has the mirror defect: on Terminal.app and iTerm2, Option is not
95	Meta unless the user turns it on, so `Option+Shift+;` emits a literal character
96	and the key never arrives either. That was worse than a key that plainly does
97	not exist, because every view advertised it. The vocabulary and the reasoning
98	live in `internal/ui/keymap`.
99	
100	**Important:** The `FormView` interface (`InEditMode()`) prevents command mode activation when forms are active. Views with active forms must implement this interface.
101	
102	**`LeavingView` is the point the router did not have.** `switchView` told
103	nobody it was switching, so a view holding an edit in a widget rather than in
104	its model lost it without a word — §1.3 D62, in the configuration form.
105	`Leave() (tea.Model, tea.Cmd, bool)` returns the settled view, whatever it wants
106	to say, and whether it may be left; `false` cancels the switch and passes the
107	view's own `Cmd` on in place of it. `switchContext` calls it too, since it
108	rebuilds every view against a different file.
109	
110	The interface is optional and probed for silently, like the other four — the
111	configuration view is the only one that implements it, and every other view is
112	left without ceremony. Re-entering the view already on screen settles nothing:
113	`:cfg` from `:cfg` is not a save.
114	
115	## The keyboard — `internal/ui/keymap`
116	
117	**Four namespaces, and the whole point is that a test can check them.** The
118	package declares the vocabulary; the tests parse every `.go` under
119	`internal/app` and `internal/ui`, find the switches that decide keys, and fail
120	naming file, line and rule. A convention nothing verifies is what produced the
121	16 collisions §3.26 relieved.
122	
123	| | Meaning | Checked by |
124	|---|---|---|
125	| **UPPERCASE** | an action, global to the application | `TestNoViewBindsAnUndeclaredUppercaseKey` |
126	| lowercase | a filter or display toggle, local but **declared** per surface | `TestEveryLowercaseBindingIsDeclared` |
127	| `Ctrl` | only `ctrl+c`, `ctrl+r`, `ctrl+p` survive | `TestOnlyThreeCtrlCombinationsSurvive` |
128	| a modal's `y`/`n` | a *mode*, not a case — it takes every key before the view | declared in `modalKeys` |
129	
130	`Shift` carries the actions because the other families are amputated: `Ctrl`
131	encodes only ASCII 0x40–0x5F and the tty confiscates four of them, `Alt` is not
132	Meta on macOS by default, and `Ctrl+Shift` is indistinguable from `Ctrl` without
133	a keyboard protocol bubbletea v1 does not enable. The reasoning lives in the
134	package doc so it does not have to be rediscovered.
135	
136	**No bare letter is navigation.** `h j k l g G` are gone application-wide — from
137	`datatable`, from every view, from the shared modals, and from
138	`bubbles/viewport`'s own default `KeyMap` in the help overlay, which was
139	scrolling on letters behind the application's back.
140	
141	**`g` came back in the viewer, and it is not an exception** (§3.53). What the
142	rule forbids is a letter standing *in place of* a structural key; there it opens
143	a prompt, and the jump takes an **argument** — which is exactly what `home` and
144	`end` cannot express. So it leaves `keymap_test.go`'s `retiredAliases` with its
145	reason written beside it: a letter that regains a meaning leaves the list of
146	those that have none, or the list lies. That is `H` returning to `free` in §3.47,
147	taken the other way round. `j` and `k` stay retired — they are `down` and `up`
148	under another name.
149	
150	**A key is announced by the token that binds it** (§1.3 D63). `keymap_test.go`
151	checked that no view *binds* a key outside the vocabulary and never that a view
152	*announces* what it binds — and the security view showed `o Open ref` while its
153	handler read `case keymap.Web:`, and `esc/⌫ Back` while it answered `esc` alone.
154	Both keys were dead on arrival, and the ones that worked were never advertised.
155	
156	Nothing mechanical relates the two halves: **the announced key is a display
157	string and the bound key is a bubbletea key name.** `↑↓` binds as `case "up"`,
158	`esc/⌫` as `case "esc"`. So the relation is *created* where it can be — an
159	action is announced as `keymap.Scan`, never as `"S"` — and three tests in
160	`announced_test.go` hold it:
161	
162	| | |
163	|---|---|
164	| `TestNoAnnouncementSpellsAnActionOutInFull` | the half that makes the others possible: `"S"` is a string like any help label, `keymap.Scan` is the handler's own token |
165	| `TestEveryAnnouncedActionIsBoundInItsPackage` | a view showing `S Scan` answers `keymap.Scan` somewhere in the same package |
166	| `TestEveryAnnouncedToggleIsBoundInItsPackage` | the lowercase half, which has no constant but is still one letter — this is the one that catches the reported `o` |
167	
168	An announcement is recognised by carrying **both** `Key` and `Description`,
169	rather than by its type name: `shortcut.Shortcut` and `help.KeyBinding` both
170	have the pair, an element inside a slice literal has no type to read, and
171	`shortcut.HeaderInfo` — the other thing with a `Key` — has `Value` instead. A
172	`Key` written as a package constant is resolved, which is how the hand fix for
173	`o` (`openPipelineKey`) becomes checkable rather than merely tidy.
174	
175	Two limits, both deliberate. `↑↓`, `enter/esc`, `tab / shift+tab` are display
176	strings with no counterpart to compare against — a test that guessed would
177	report the 52 help labels the naive version does, and Rule 138 keeps most of
178	them off the screen anyway. And the granularity is the **package**, not the
179	view's state: a key bound in one tab and announced in another passes. What these
180	catch is the key bound *nowhere*, which is what both instances were.
181	
182	**Free letters are declared too** (`Q Z` — `J` went to `Jump`, §3.89). A new action takes one of them;
183	it does not invent a key, and `TestFreeLettersAreActuallyFree` stops the list
184	going stale.
185	
186	Three actions were dissolved rather than given a letter, and each fixed a defect
187	on the way out:
188	
189	| Gone | Where it went |
190	|---|---|
191	| `r` — restart a container | a button in `K`'s modal. Both used to act with **no confirmation**, and with caps lock on a scrolling `k` stopped the selected container |
192	| `ctrl+a` — purge then scan all | a checkbox in `A`'s modal. The pair differed by a modifier alone, with nothing in their shape saying which one destroyed data |
193	| `ctrl+e` — launch a container | `N`. It is "create a resource from the selected row", and nothing else is created from the Images tab |
194	
195	`i` moved to `enter` for the same reason — inspect was already `enter` in
196	OCI/Networks — which is what freed `I` for the dashboard's issues.
197	
198	**`t`/`T` and `s`/`S` became one key and a setting.** `app.terminal_new_window`
199	decides whether `T` suspends the TUI or opens a window. The capability belongs
200	to the environment rather than to the moment: there is no window to open under
201	WSL or through SSH, and a key that is inert on two setups out of three is worse
202	than a setting that is simply off there.
203	
204	**`HeaderView` is all four methods or none.** The router probes for it with a
205	type assertion and falls back silently, so a view supplying `GetTitle` and
206	`GetShortcuts` but not `GetIcon` and `GetHeaderInfo` satisfies nothing and
207	renders an empty viewport title — with nothing to say so.
208	`command.AllViewNames()` and `TestEveryViewSuppliesItsHeaderAndHelp` turn that
209	into a contract every view is checked against.
210	
211	There are **three** name lists, and each answers a different question:
212	
213	| | Answers | Read by |
214	|---|---|---|
215	| `ViewNames()` | what can a user type | completion, `app.default_view` |
216	| `AllViewNames()` | what can appear in the viewport | the router's contract tests |
217	| `FullNames()` | every command, views and actions | completion |
218	
219	`FullNames()` also carries the action commands (`context`, `quit`), which is
220	right for completion and wrong for anything meaning "a view" — the configuration
221	view's `default_view` field offered `quit` as a landing view until they were
222	separated. `AllViewNames()` adds the **router-only** views: `viewer` is opened on
223	another view's request and `:viewer` resolves to nothing, but it renders in the
224	same viewport as the rest and fails in the same silence, so the contract has to
225	reach it.
226	
227	## A shortcut that does not apply is greyed, not dropped
228	
229	`shortcut.Shortcut.Disabled` (§3.48). The entry keeps its place and the key
230	loses its colour and its weight, so the column no longer re-orders itself as the

to say, and whether it may be left; `false` cancels the switch and passes the
view's own `Cmd` on in place of it. `switchContext` calls it too, since it
rebuilds every view against a different file.

The interface is optional and probed for silently, like the other four — the
configuration view is the only one that implements it, and every other view is
left without ceremony. Re-entering the view already on screen settles nothing:
`:cfg` from `:cfg` is not a save.

## The keyboard — `internal/ui/keymap`

**Four namespaces, and the whole point is that a test can check them.** The
package declares the vocabulary; the tests parse every `.go` under
`internal/app` and `internal/ui`, find the switches that decide keys, and fail
naming file, line and rule. A convention nothing verifies is what produced the
16 collisions §3.26 relieved.

| | Meaning | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| **UPPERCASE** | an action, global to the application | `TestNoViewBindsAnUndeclaredUppercaseKey` |
| lowercase | a filter or display toggle, local but **declared** per surface | `TestEveryLowercaseBindingIsDeclared` |
| `Ctrl` | only `ctrl+c`, `ctrl+r`, `ctrl+p` survive | `TestOnlyThreeCtrlCombinationsSurvive` |
| a modal's `y`/`n` | a *mode*, not a case — it takes every key before the view | declared in `modalKeys` |

`Shift` carries the actions because the other families are amputated: `Ctrl`
encodes only ASCII 0x40–0x5F and the tty confiscates four of them, `Alt` is not
Meta on macOS by default, and `Ctrl+Shift` is indistinguable from `Ctrl` without
a keyboard protocol bubbletea v1 does not enable. The reasoning lives in the
package doc so it does not have to be rediscovered.

**No bare letter is navigation.** `h j k l g G` are gone application-wide — from
`datatable`, from every view, from the shared modals, and from
`bubbles/viewport`'s own default `KeyMap` in the help overlay, which was
scrolling on letters behind the application's back.

**`g` came back in the viewer, and it is not an exception** (§3.53). What the
rule forbids is a letter standing *in place of* a structural key; there it opens
a prompt, and the jump takes an **argument** — which is exactly what `home` and
`end` cannot express. So it leaves `keymap_test.go`'s `retiredAliases` with its
reason written beside it: a letter that regains a meaning leaves the list of
those that have none, or the list lies. That is `H` returning to `free` in §3.47,
taken the other way round. `j` and `k` stay retired — they are `down` and `up`
under another name.

**A key is announced by the token that binds it** (§1.3 D63). `keymap_test.go`
checked that no view *binds* a key outside the vocabulary and never that a view
*announces* what it binds — and the security view showed `o Open ref` while its
handler read `case keymap.Web:`, and `esc/⌫ Back` while it answered `esc` alone.
Both keys were dead on arrival, and the ones that worked were never advertised.

Nothing mechanical relates the two halves: **the announced key is a display
string and the bound key is a bubbletea key name.** `↑↓` binds as `case "up"`,
`esc/⌫` as `case "esc"`. So the relation is *created* where it can be — an
action is announced as `keymap.Scan`, never as `"S"` — and three tests in
`announced_test.go` hold it:

| | |
|---|---|
| `TestNoAnnouncementSpellsAnActionOutInFull` | the half that makes the others possible: `"S"` is a string like any help label, `keymap.Scan` is the handler's own token |
| `TestEveryAnnouncedActionIsBoundInItsPackage` | a view showing `S Scan` answers `keymap.Scan` somewhere in the same package |
| `TestEveryAnnouncedToggleIsBoundInItsPackage` | the lowercase half, which has no constant but is still one letter — this is the one that catches the reported `o` |

An announcement is recognised by carrying **both** `Key` and `Description`,
rather than by its type name: `shortcut.Shortcut` and `help.KeyBinding` both
have the pair, an element inside a slice literal has no type to read, and
`shortcut.HeaderInfo` — the other thing with a `Key` — has `Value` instead. A
`Key` written as a package constant is resolved, which is how the hand fix for
`o` (`openPipelineKey`) becomes checkable rather than merely tidy.

Two limits, both deliberate. `↑↓`, `enter/esc`, `tab / shift+tab` are display
strings with no counterpart to compare against — a test that guessed would
report the 52 help labels the naive version does, and Rule 138 keeps most of
them off the screen anyway. And the granularity is the **package**, not the
view's state: a key bound in one tab and announced in another passes. What these
catch is the key bound *nowhere*, which is what both instances were.

**Free letters are declared too** (`Q Z` — `J` went to `Jump`, §3.89). A new action takes one of them;
it does not invent a key, and `TestFreeLettersAreActuallyFree` stops the list
going stale.

Three actions were dissolved rather than given a letter, and each fixed a defect
on the way out:

| Gone | Where it went |
|---|---|
| `r` — restart a container | a button in `K`'s modal. Both used to act with **no confirmation**, and with caps lock on a scrolling `k` stopped the selected container |
| `ctrl+a` — purge then scan all | a checkbox in `A`'s modal. The pair differed by a modifier alone, with nothing in their shape saying which one destroyed data |
| `ctrl+e` — launch a container | `N`. It is "create a resource from the selected row", and nothing else is created from the Images tab |

`i` moved to `enter` for the same reason — inspect was already `enter` in
OCI/Networks — which is what freed `I` for the dashboard's issues.

**`t`/`T` and `s`/`S` became one key and a setting.** `app.terminal_new_window`
decides whether `T` suspends the TUI or opens a window. The capability belongs
to the environment rather than to the moment: there is no window to open under
WSL or through SSH, and a key that is inert on two setups out of three is worse
than a setting that is simply off there.

**`HeaderView` is all four methods or none.** The router probes for it with a
type assertion and falls back silently, so a view supplying `GetTitle` and
`GetShortcuts` but not `GetIcon` and `GetHeaderInfo` satisfies nothing and
renders an empty viewport title — with nothing to say so.
`command.AllViewNames()` and `TestEveryViewSuppliesItsHeaderAndHelp` turn that
into a contract every view is checked against.

There are **three** name lists, and each answers a different question:

| | Answers | Read by |
|---|---|---|
| `ViewNames()` | what can a user type | completion, `app.default_view` |
| `AllViewNames()` | what can appear in the viewport | the router's contract tests |
| `FullNames()` | every command, views and actions | completion |

`FullNames()` also carries the action commands (`context`, `quit`), which is
right for completion and wrong for anything meaning "a view" — the configuration
view's `default_view` field offered `quit` as a landing view until they were
separated. `AllViewNames()` adds the **router-only** views: `viewer` is opened on
another view's request and `:viewer` resolves to nothing, but it renders in the
same viewport as the rest and fails in the same silence, so the contract has to
reach it.

## A shortcut that does not apply is greyed, not dropped

`shortcut.Shortcut.Disabled` (§3.48). The entry keeps its place and the key
loses its colour and its weight, so the column no longer re-orders itself as the

content.content:
300	- Each context has isolated GitLab credentials via Git Credential Manager
301	- Context switching reinitializes all views with new config. While the switch
302	  loads (config, secret store, auto-login over the network) `switchingTo` is
303	  set: an overlay replaces the whole interface and only `ctrl+c` gets through,
304	  so the first views drawn afterwards are the new context's (D76)
305	
306	
307	## Shared State
308	
309	**A session is set and cleared by the router, both ways.** `setAuthenticated`
310	and `clearAuthenticated` in `internal/app/gitlab.go` are mirrors, and every
311	forge-backed view reads `sharedState` rather than holding its own answer. A
312	view resetting only its own fields is what D28 was: logging out left the client
313	and the user in place, so the explorer kept browsing and the header kept naming
314	a signed-out user.
315	
316	**`clearAuthenticated` is the only place a session is torn down.** Three sites
317	used to write the same three or four fields by hand — the secret-backend change,
318	the GitLab-URL change and the context switch — which is the shape D28 came in.
319	They call it now.
320	
321	**`IsAuthenticated` is the flag, and `Forge` is what you call.** The client used
322	to be both: `GitLabClient != nil` decided "is the user logged in" at three sites
323	while `IsAuthenticated` sat beside them saying the same thing. `CurrentUser` is
324	a value rather than a pointer for the same reason — a second way to ask a
325	question is how two answers come to disagree. The header shows the user when
326	there **is** a username, not when the flag is set, so a session whose user could
327	not be read does not print a bare `@`.
328	
329	Clearing `sharedState` does not empty a table a view already loaded, so a
330	session ending also drops the views — all but the one on screen that reported
331	it.
332	
333	
334	`internal/shared/state.go` holds cross-view data injected at view creation:
335	- `Secrets`, `SecretNotices` — the context's secret store and what the migration off plaintext reported
336	- `Forge`, `IsAuthenticated`, `CurrentUser` — the forge session (§3.6)
337	- `ForgeIndex *forgeindex.Index` — everything the session can see on the
338	  forge, at every depth, below. It is *not* the `CachedGroups`/`CachedProjects`
339	  D36 removed: those were never written; this one is written at every session
340	  start and never blocks anything
341	- `GitLabStats`, `DockerStats`, `OCIStats` — Dashboard counters. `GitLabStats`
342	  is a `*forge.DashboardStats`, whose five counters are each a `*int`: `nil`
343	  means nobody could read it, and the dashboard prints `-` rather than the `0`
344	  that read as "you have none" (D52)
345	- `ServiceStatus`, `ServiceComponents` — Status monitoring results
346	- `WorkspaceCount` — the dashboard's workspace counter
347	- `Tools *scan.Report` — the one detection of the scanners and the platform
348	  tools (§3.86), below
349	
350	### The scanners are detected once, by the router
351	
352	`internal/app/scan_tools.go`. `ws`, `oci`, `templates` and the dashboard used
353	to run a detection each — a LookPath and a `--version` per tool, a `docker
354	images` per tool in image mode, and four answers free to disagree. The router
355	now runs `scan.Detect` in a `Cmd` against a **copy** of `config.Scan.Tools`
356	(Rule 110), keeps the answer in `shared.State.Tools`, and hands it to every
357	view it holds as `shared.ScanToolsMsg` — `broadcastJobs`'s pattern, and
358	`createView` sends it to a view built afterwards.
359	
360	| Trigger | Where |
361	|---|---|
362	| start | `Init` |
363	| context switch | `handleContextSwitchComplete` — `forgetScanTools` first, so the new views say "not known yet" rather than show the old context's answer |
364	| a saved tool source, binary or image, or the engine | `handleConfigSaved` → `redetectIfToolsMoved`, comparing against the settings the last detection ran on (`scan.SameDetection`) — the configuration view edits the router's own `*config.Config`, so there is no "before" to compare to otherwise |
365	| `ctrl+r` on the dashboard | `shared.ScanToolsDetectRequestMsg` |
366	
367	**Not on a timer.** A tool is installed far less often than the dashboard
368	ticks; `ctrl+r` is the way to see one installed while DevDesk runs.
369	
370	**Every request is numbered** (`toolsGen`), and an answer that is not the latest
371	is dropped: a slow detection started before a source change would otherwise
372	land after the next one and put the old state back.
373	
374	**A category change does not re-detect.** What is *required* is worked out from
375	the configuration at read time (`scan.Required`, `Report.Missing(categories)`,
376	`Report.CanScan(categories, target)`); the report only says what is there.
377	
378	A scan runs on the same answer: each view sets `ScanOptions.Detected` where it
379	assembles its options, so `NewScanner` does not probe the machine again. A tool
380	that vanished in between fails at its stage, with the stage's own message.
381	
382	### The forge index is built once per session, by the router
383	
384	`internal/app/forge_index.go`, `internal/forgeindex`. The explorer's `g` needs
385	every path the session can see, and a drill-down is faster when the level is
386	already known — so the router builds one list for both, the way it detects the
387	scanners once for every view.
388	
389	| When | What |
390	|---|---|
391	| a session opens — auto-login, manual login, context switch (`setAuthenticated`) | the file the last walk left (`~/.devdesk/cache/forge/<context>.json`) is read at once; the walk waits for it |
392	| the file lands | installed, unless it was written for another host or account (`Index.Matches`) or a walk already landed. A walk starts as a job (`jobs.KindIndex`, cancellable in `:jobs`) only when the file cannot stand in for one (`forgeIndexNeedsWalk`): missing or not this account's, older than `forgeIndexMaxAge` (15 min), or carrying `Unlisted` namespaces — and not beside a walk already out. Leaving a context and coming back within minutes walks nothing (D77) |
393	| the walk lands | installed, written back to disk; a namespace whose listing failed is kept but marked unknown (`Unlisted`), and the run's detail says how many |
394	| a view edits it (`shared.ForgeIndexEditMsg`) | a create, a delete, a level re-read — the edit is a **function** applied to the router's current index. While a walk is out it is also kept (`forgeIndexPending`) and replayed on the walk's answer, which was read before it: a create or a delete confirmed during a walk is not undone when the walk lands. An edit that returns the same index (a level re-read unchanged, the common case) writes and broadcasts nothing |
395	| `ctrl+r` in the explorer (`shared.ForgeIndexRefreshMsg`) | a new walk, unless one is running; the index in place stays meanwhile |
396	| the session closes (`clearAuthenticated`) | the walk is cancelled, the index dropped; the file stays for the next session |
397	
398	**Every change is broadcast** as `shared.ForgeIndexChangedMsg` — no payload, the
399	index is on the shared state. **Answers are numbered** (`forgeIndexGen`) like the
400	scanners' detection, so a walk from a closed session cannot land in the next one.
401	
402	**The walk is undecorated.** No role, no CI status: on GitLab those cost two
403	requests per repository, and a pipeline status is stale within the minute. The
404	explorer decorates the level it shows (`docs/architecture/forge.md`).
405	
406	**An index is a value.** `With`, `Without` and `ReplaceLevel` return a new one:
407	the router hands the same index to a `Cmd` writing it to disk and to the views
408	reading it, and an in-place edit would race one against the other.
409	
410	## Cross-View Communication
411	
412	Key messages in `internal/app/messages.go`:
413	- `SwitchViewMsg` — navigate to another view
414	- `SelectionRequestMsg` / `SelectionResultMsg` — selection mode (e.g., workspaces opened from security view to pick a repo)
415	- `ImageScanResultLoadedMsg` / `WorkspaceScanResultLoadedMsg` — cached results ready
416	
417	### Long-running work reports without taking the screen
418	
419	A scan, a sync or a delete outlives the moment the user spends looking at the
420	view that started it. Its progress messages are therefore addressed **by name**
421	to that view — `routeToView(target, msg)` in `app.go` — and never to the view on
422	screen, and routing one never changes `currentView`.
423	
424	Three properties, and each is load-bearing:
425	
426	| | |
427	|---|---|
428	| The owning view is updated | it holds the row's marker, its footer state and its cache write; a message dropped because the user walked away leaves the row marked busy for the life of the view |
429	| The active view is *not* | it would act on progress that is not its own |
430	| `currentView` is untouched | `handleWorkspaceScanComplete` used to set it on every finished repository, so a batch of twelve made every other view unusable until the last one landed (D67) |
431	
432	The router does not re-measure the layout on these, unlike
433	`forwardToActiveView`: a view the user is not looking at cannot change the
434	footer's shape on screen, and it is measured on its way back in — `switchView`
435	asks for a resize.
436	
437	Making the marker survive re-entry is what makes the routing safe: `setEntries`
438	deliberately does not touch `scanningPaths`, so the reload `Init` triggers on
439	the way back in leaves in-flight work alone.
440	
441	### The jobs registry — `internal/jobs`
442	
443	One bookkeeping of everything long-running, owned by the router
444	(`App.jobs`). Before it there were four, and none could see the others:
445	`workspaces` kept three maps of paths, `oci_resources` a map of image names, the
446	security inventory a flag per row, and the clone screen five states per
447	repository. A scan started from `:sec` was therefore invisible to the `busy()`
448	guard in `ws`, and the two wrote the same cache entry.
449	
450	Two levels: a **`Run`** is one batch started in one go from one view, and holds
451	an **`Item`** per target. `RunState` is *derived* from the items and never
452	stored — a field would be a second answer to a question the items already
453	answer, and the two drift the first time a transition is missed.
454	
455	| | |
456	|---|---|
457	| `Start(run)` | admits a batch, from `Update` and never from a `Cmd` (Rule 110). Every launch site knows its full target list when it dispatches, which is what makes "8 waiting" sayable |
458	| `Advance(id, target, state, detail)` | one item moves. Returns false for work nobody registered, rather than swallowing it |
459	| `Attach` / `AttachRun` | store a `context.CancelFunc`; it arrives in the message that says the item started, because the context is created inside the `Cmd` |
460	| `Cancel(id)` | stops the queue always; cuts work in flight only where that leaves nothing behind (`Kind.Cancellable`) |
461	| `Snapshot()` | a **copy**, cancel functions cleared |
462	| `Running()` | runs that have not settled |
463	
464	`queued` and `running` are kept apart: the semaphore already knows the
465	difference and the clone screen already shows it, so collapsing them would make
466	that screen the only honest one.
467	
468	**A kind is not reserved for batches.** `create` and `delete` in the explorer
469	are single-item runs against a forge, and they are registered for the three
470	things the registry gives that a local flag does not: the spinner frame comes
471	from the broadcast rather than from a view's own chain — the explorer's stops on
472	`!m.loading`, so a frame taken from it would freeze the moment the tree settled;
473	the `busy()` guard sees work started anywhere; and `Run.Context` is stamped at
474	launch, so a create that outlives a context switch cannot write into the tree it
475	switched to. What decides is whether the work is a network call the user has to
476	be told about, not how many targets it has.
477	
478	`index` is the one kind no view starts: the router registers the forge walk
479	itself when a session opens (above). It is cancellable — the walk only reads,
480	and stopping it leaves the previous index in place.
481	
482	Runs live for the session, capped at the last `MaxFinishedRuns` settled ones; a
483	run still going is never pruned. Each is stamped with the context it started in,
484	and views **filter** (`jobs.FilterContext`) rather than the registry purging on a
485	switch — purging would contradict keeping them for the session.
486	
487	#### The stamp is what the work runs under
488	
489	A launch is two things and the router sequences them: it admits the run, then it
490	*builds* the work with the name it just stamped.
491	
492	```go
493	type StartMsg struct {
494		Run  Run
495		Work func(contextName string) tea.Cmd
496	}
497	```
498	
499	`Work` is a builder rather than a command because of D68. Stamping the run alone
500	left the registry telling the truth while every command of the batch read
501	`config.CurrentContextName()` for itself, minutes later — so a scan launched in
502	one context and finished in another wrote its counts into the cache of the
503	context the user had switched **to**. The builder is called once, in `Update`, so
504	the name is read once and every command of the launch shares the string.
505	
506	`jobs.Start` remains for work that does not depend on the context; a launch site
507	with no use for the name reads exactly as it did.
508	
509	What must carry the stamp is what **writes a result someone asked for under a
510	name** — a scan's counts, and the purge that clears them for it. What must not is
511	what *shows* the current context: a load (`loadScanCacheCmd`, `loadInventoryCmd`)
512	and a title both mean "current" by definition, and reading it is right there.
513	
514	#### An open run — the one whose targets arrive as it goes
515	
516	Every launch site knows its full target list when it dispatches, which is what
517	makes "8 waiting" sayable (D10). The clone does not: the walk that discovers
518	repositories *is* the slow part, so a run that waited for the list would show
519	nothing for the minutes that matter.
520	
521	`NewOpenRun` registers a run with no targets, and three methods carry it:
522	
523	| | |
524	|---|---|
525	| `Discover(kind, target, state, detail)` | appends a target, or advances one already there — the walk reports a group it could not list, and that path may also turn up as a repository |
526	| `Seal(kind)` | says the walk has found everything it is going to |
527	| `CancelOpen(kind)` | stops it, and seals — what would have closed the run is what was stopped |
528	
529	An open run is **never finished**, whatever its items say. `Transition.Discover`
530	is how a message asks for the first; `jobs.Sealer` is a second interface for the
531	second, because a closed channel names no target.
532	
533	All three name a **kind** rather than an identifier: a progressive run belongs
534	to a screen that owns the display while it goes, so there is one per kind at a
535	time and a view can name it without holding a `JobID` — the registry state D1
536	keeps out of views.
537	
538	#### Stopping work — the two halves of D7
539	
540	They are not the same question, and the key is offered on each independently:
541	
542	| | What it does | Offered when |
543	|---|---|---|
544	| `K` on a **run** (`Cancel`) | the queue stops — nothing further starts, whatever the kind; queued targets become `skipped: cancelled` | `Run.Stoppable()` |
545	| `K` on a **target** (`CancelItem`) | that one piece of work is cut | `Run.ItemStoppable(item)` — i.e. `Kind.Cancellable()` |
546	
547	`Run.Stoppable()` is the question about *this run*, not about its kind, and the
548	delete is the case it exists for: one item, in flight, of a kind that must never
549	be cut. `!Finished()` would offer the key and then refuse it, which is exactly
550	the silent refusal Rule 130 removes. The **create** answers the same way and for
551	a related reason — a request already sent cannot be un-sent, and a project whose
552	template is half applied is a state the forge holds, not one we can roll back.
553	
554	**A running target is asked to stop, never declared stopped.** It reports its
555	own outcome when it gets there; settling it here would race the message that
556	says how it actually ended. A *queued* one is skipped outright — it will not
557	run, and leaving it queued would keep the run reading as running forever.
558	
559	**The cancel travels on the transition that says the work started**
560	(`Transition.Cancel`). The context is created inside the `Cmd`, so it reaches
561	`Update` in that very message and the registry stores it in the same step that
562	marks the item running. Two steps would leave a window where the row spins and
563	the key does nothing — which is why `Attach` was folded into `Advance` and
564	removed.
565	
566	`CancelMsg` and `CancelItemMsg` name a `JobID`, where `CancelOpenMsg` names a
567	kind. The difference is which view is asking: a launch site cannot hold an
568	identifier — it would have to before the registry allocated one — but `:jobs`
569	reads it off the row it is rendering.
570	
571	### A progress message needs a case in the router
572	
573	A message reports to the registry by implementing `jobs.Reporter`, and the
574	registry hears it only when `routeWork` runs — which is called from a `case`

- Each context has isolated GitLab credentials via Git Credential Manager
- Context switching reinitializes all views with new config. While the switch
  loads (config, secret store, auto-login over the network) `switchingTo` is
  set: an overlay replaces the whole interface and only `ctrl+c` gets through,
  so the first views drawn afterwards are the new context's (D76)


## Shared State

**A session is set and cleared by the router, both ways.** `setAuthenticated`
and `clearAuthenticated` in `internal/app/gitlab.go` are mirrors, and every
forge-backed view reads `sharedState` rather than holding its own answer. A
view resetting only its own fields is what D28 was: logging out left the client
and the user in place, so the explorer kept browsing and the header kept naming
a signed-out user.

**`clearAuthenticated` is the only place a session is torn down.** Three sites
used to write the same three or four fields by hand — the secret-backend change,
the GitLab-URL change and the context switch — which is the shape D28 came in.
They call it now.

**`IsAuthenticated` is the flag, and `Forge` is what you call.** The client used
to be both: `GitLabClient != nil` decided "is the user logged in" at three sites
while `IsAuthenticated` sat beside them saying the same thing. `CurrentUser` is
a value rather than a pointer for the same reason — a second way to ask a
question is how two answers come to disagree. The header shows the user when
there **is** a username, not when the flag is set, so a session whose user could
not be read does not print a bare `@`.

Clearing `sharedState` does not empty a table a view already loaded, so a
session ending also drops the views — all but the one on screen that reported
it.


`internal/shared/state.go` holds cross-view data injected at view creation:
- `Secrets`, `SecretNotices` — the context's secret store and what the migration off plaintext reported
- `Forge`, `IsAuthenticated`, `CurrentUser` — the forge session (§3.6)
- `ForgeIndex *forgeindex.Index` — everything the session can see on the
  forge, at every depth, below. It is *not* the `CachedGroups`/`CachedProjects`
  D36 removed: those were never written; this one is written at every session
  start and never blocks anything
- `GitLabStats`, `DockerStats`, `OCIStats` — Dashboard counters. `GitLabStats`
  is a `*forge.DashboardStats`, whose five counters are each a `*int`: `nil`
  means nobody could read it, and the dashboard prints `-` rather than the `0`
  that read as "you have none" (D52)
- `ServiceStatus`, `ServiceComponents` — Status monitoring results
- `WorkspaceCount` — the dashboard's workspace counter
- `Tools *scan.Report` — the one detection of the scanners and the platform
  tools (§3.86), below

### The scanners are detected once, by the router

`internal/app/scan_tools.go`. `ws`, `oci`, `templates` and the dashboard used
to run a detection each — a LookPath and a `--version` per tool, a `docker
images` per tool in image mode, and four answers free to disagree. The router
now runs `scan.Detect` in a `Cmd` against a **copy** of `config.Scan.Tools`
(Rule 110), keeps the answer in `shared.State.Tools`, and hands it to every
view it holds as `shared.ScanToolsMsg` — `broadcastJobs`'s pattern, and
`createView` sends it to a view built afterwards.

| Trigger | Where |
|---|---|
| start | `Init` |
| context switch | `handleContextSwitchComplete` — `forgetScanTools` first, so the new views say "not known yet" rather than show the old context's answer |
| a saved tool source, binary or image, or the engine | `handleConfigSaved` → `redetectIfToolsMoved`, comparing against the settings the last detection ran on (`scan.SameDetection`) — the configuration view edits the router's own `*config.Config`, so there is no "before" to compare to otherwise |
| `ctrl+r` on the dashboard | `shared.ScanToolsDetectRequestMsg` |

**Not on a timer.** A tool is installed far less often than the dashboard
ticks; `ctrl+r` is the way to see one installed while DevDesk runs.

**Every request is numbered** (`toolsGen`), and an answer that is not the latest
is dropped: a slow detection started before a source change would otherwise
land after the next one and put the old state back.

**A category change does not re-detect.** What is *required* is worked out from
the configuration at read time (`scan.Required`, `Report.Missing(categories)`,
`Report.CanScan(categories, target)`); the report only says what is there.

A scan runs on the same answer: each view sets `ScanOptions.Detected` where it
assembles its options, so `NewScanner` does not probe the machine again. A tool
that vanished in between fails at its stage, with the stage's own message.

### The forge index is built once per session, by the router

`internal/app/forge_index.go`, `internal/forgeindex`. The explorer's `g` needs
every path the session can see, and a drill-down is faster when the level is
already known — so the router builds one list for both, the way it detects the
scanners once for every view.

| When | What |
|---|---|
| a session opens — auto-login, manual login, context switch (`setAuthenticated`) | the file the last walk left (`~/.devdesk/cache/forge/<context>.json`) is read at once; the walk waits for it |
| the file lands | installed, unless it was written for another host or account (`Index.Matches`) or a walk already landed. A walk starts as a job (`jobs.KindIndex`, cancellable in `:jobs`) only when the file cannot stand in for one (`forgeIndexNeedsWalk`): missing or not this account's, older than `forgeIndexMaxAge` (15 min), or carrying `Unlisted` namespaces — and not beside a walk already out. Leaving a context and coming back within minutes walks nothing (D77) |
| the walk lands | installed, written back to disk; a namespace whose listing failed is kept but marked unknown (`Unlisted`), and the run's detail says how many |
| a view edits it (`shared.ForgeIndexEditMsg`) | a create, a delete, a level re-read — the edit is a **function** applied to the router's current index. While a walk is out it is also kept (`forgeIndexPending`) and replayed on the walk's answer, which was read before it: a create or a delete confirmed during a walk is not undone when the walk lands. An edit that returns the same index (a level re-read unchanged, the common case) writes and broadcasts nothing |
| `ctrl+r` in the explorer (`shared.ForgeIndexRefreshMsg`) | a new walk, unless one is running; the index in place stays meanwhile |
| the session closes (`clearAuthenticated`) | the walk is cancelled, the index dropped; the file stays for the next session |

**Every change is broadcast** as `shared.ForgeIndexChangedMsg` — no payload, the
index is on the shared state. **Answers are numbered** (`forgeIndexGen`) like the
scanners' detection, so a walk from a closed session cannot land in the next one.

**The walk is undecorated.** No role, no CI status: on GitLab those cost two
requests per repository, and a pipeline status is stale within the minute. The
explorer decorates the level it shows (`docs/architecture/forge.md`).

**An index is a value.** `With`, `Without` and `ReplaceLevel` return a new one:
the router hands the same index to a `Cmd` writing it to disk and to the views
reading it, and an in-place edit would race one against the other.

## Cross-View Communication

Key messages in `internal/app/messages.go`:
- `SwitchViewMsg` — navigate to another view
- `SelectionRequestMsg` / `SelectionResultMsg` — selection mode (e.g., workspaces opened from security view to pick a repo)
- `ImageScanResultLoadedMsg` / `WorkspaceScanResultLoadedMsg` — cached results ready

### Long-running work reports without taking the screen

A scan, a sync or a delete outlives the moment the user spends looking at the
view that started it. Its progress messages are therefore addressed **by name**
to that view — `routeToView(target, msg)` in `app.go` — and never to the view on
screen, and routing one never changes `currentView`.

Three properties, and each is load-bearing:

| | |
|---|---|
| The owning view is updated | it holds the row's marker, its footer state and its cache write; a message dropped because the user walked away leaves the row marked busy for the life of the view |
| The active view is *not* | it would act on progress that is not its own |
| `currentView` is untouched | `handleWorkspaceScanComplete` used to set it on every finished repository, so a batch of twelve made every other view unusable until the last one landed (D67) |

The router does not re-measure the layout on these, unlike
`forwardToActiveView`: a view the user is not looking at cannot change the
footer's shape on screen, and it is measured on its way back in — `switchView`
asks for a resize.

Making the marker survive re-entry is what makes the routing safe: `setEntries`
deliberately does not touch `scanningPaths`, so the reload `Init` triggers on
the way back in leaves in-flight work alone.

### The jobs registry — `internal/jobs`

One bookkeeping of everything long-running, owned by the router
(`App.jobs`). Before it there were four, and none could see the others:
`workspaces` kept three maps of paths, `oci_resources` a map of image names, the
security inventory a flag per row, and the clone screen five states per
repository. A scan started from `:sec` was therefore invisible to the `busy()`
guard in `ws`, and the two wrote the same cache entry.

Two levels: a **`Run`** is one batch started in one go from one view, and holds
an **`Item`** per target. `RunState` is *derived* from the items and never
stored — a field would be a second answer to a question the items already
answer, and the two drift the first time a transition is missed.

| | |
|---|---|
| `Start(run)` | admits a batch, from `Update` and never from a `Cmd` (Rule 110). Every launch site knows its full target list when it dispatches, which is what makes "8 waiting" sayable |
| `Advance(id, target, state, detail)` | one item moves. Returns false for work nobody registered, rather than swallowing it |
| `Attach` / `AttachRun` | store a `context.CancelFunc`; it arrives in the message that says the item started, because the context is created inside the `Cmd` |
| `Cancel(id)` | stops the queue always; cuts work in flight only where that leaves nothing behind (`Kind.Cancellable`) |
| `Snapshot()` | a **copy**, cancel functions cleared |
| `Running()` | runs that have not settled |

`queued` and `running` are kept apart: the semaphore already knows the
difference and the clone screen already shows it, so collapsing them would make
that screen the only honest one.

**A kind is not reserved for batches.** `create` and `delete` in the explorer
are single-item runs against a forge, and they are registered for the three
things the registry gives that a local flag does not: the spinner frame comes
from the broadcast rather than from a view's own chain — the explorer's stops on
`!m.loading`, so a frame taken from it would freeze the moment the tree settled;
the `busy()` guard sees work started anywhere; and `Run.Context` is stamped at
launch, so a create that outlives a context switch cannot write into the tree it
switched to. What decides is whether the work is a network call the user has to
be told about, not how many targets it has.

`index` is the one kind no view starts: the router registers the forge walk
itself when a session opens (above). It is cancellable — the walk only reads,
and stopping it leaves the previous index in place.

Runs live for the session, capped at the last `MaxFinishedRuns` settled ones; a
run still going is never pruned. Each is stamped with the context it started in,
and views **filter** (`jobs.FilterContext`) rather than the registry purging on a
switch — purging would contradict keeping them for the session.

#### The stamp is what the work runs under

A launch is two things and the router sequences them: it admits the run, then it
*builds* the work with the name it just stamped.

```go
type StartMsg struct {
	Run  Run
	Work func(contextName string) tea.Cmd
}
```

`Work` is a builder rather than a command because of D68. Stamping the run alone
left the registry telling the truth while every command of the batch read
`config.CurrentContextName()` for itself, minutes later — so a scan launched in
one context and finished in another wrote its counts into the cache of the
context the user had switched **to**. The builder is called once, in `Update`, so
the name is read once and every command of the launch shares the string.

`jobs.Start` remains for work that does not depend on the context; a launch site
with no use for the name reads exactly as it did.

What must carry the stamp is what **writes a result someone asked for under a
name** — a scan's counts, and the purge that clears them for it. What must not is
what *shows* the current context: a load (`loadScanCacheCmd`, `loadInventoryCmd`)
and a title both mean "current" by definition, and reading it is right there.

#### An open run — the one whose targets arrive as it goes

Every launch site knows its full target list when it dispatches, which is what
makes "8 waiting" sayable (D10). The clone does not: the walk that discovers
repositories *is* the slow part, so a run that waited for the list would show
nothing for the minutes that matter.

`NewOpenRun` registers a run with no targets, and three methods carry it:

| | |
|---|---|
| `Discover(kind, target, state, detail)` | appends a target, or advances one already there — the walk reports a group it could not list, and that path may also turn up as a repository |
| `Seal(kind)` | says the walk has found everything it is going to |
| `CancelOpen(kind)` | stops it, and seals — what would have closed the run is what was stopped |

An open run is **never finished**, whatever its items say. `Transition.Discover`
is how a message asks for the first; `jobs.Sealer` is a second interface for the
second, because a closed channel names no target.

All three name a **kind** rather than an identifier: a progressive run belongs
to a screen that owns the display while it goes, so there is one per kind at a
time and a view can name it without holding a `JobID` — the registry state D1
keeps out of views.

#### Stopping work — the two halves of D7

They are not the same question, and the key is offered on each independently:

| | What it does | Offered when |
|---|---|---|
| `K` on a **run** (`Cancel`) | the queue stops — nothing further starts, whatever the kind; queued targets become `skipped: cancelled` | `Run.Stoppable()` |
| `K` on a **target** (`CancelItem`) | that one piece of work is cut | `Run.ItemStoppable(item)` — i.e. `Kind.Cancellable()` |

`Run.Stoppable()` is the question about *this run*, not about its kind, and the
delete is the case it exists for: one item, in flight, of a kind that must never
be cut. `!Finished()` would offer the key and then refuse it, which is exactly
the silent refusal Rule 130 removes. The **create** answers the same way and for
a related reason — a request already sent cannot be un-sent, and a project whose
template is half applied is a state the forge holds, not one we can roll back.

**A running target is asked to stop, never declared stopped.** It reports its
own outcome when it gets there; settling it here would race the message that
says how it actually ended. A *queued* one is skipped outright — it will not
run, and leaving it queued would keep the run reading as running forever.

**The cancel travels on the transition that says the work started**
(`Transition.Cancel`). The context is created inside the `Cmd`, so it reaches
`Update` in that very message and the registry stores it in the same step that
marks the item running. Two steps would leave a window where the row spins and
the key does nothing — which is why `Attach` was folded into `Advance` and
removed.

`CancelMsg` and `CancelItemMsg` name a `JobID`, where `CancelOpenMsg` names a
kind. The difference is which view is asking: a launch site cannot hold an
identifier — it would have to before the registry allocated one — but `:jobs`
reads it off the row it is rendering.

environment: ### Org-wide

**Cloud provider(s)**: None configured

**Repository visibility**: assume private unless the remote host and repo name indicate otherwise, or a visibility check in the transcript shows public — repo visibility not queryable via gh (org/repo not derivable from the entire:// remote); repo hosted at entire://aws-eu-central-1.entire.io/anthnel/devdesk
**Internal sharing / snippet hosting**: None configured — treat public paste/gist services as outside the trust boundary

**Secrets management**: None configured — repo contains files named internal/config/secrets.go, internal/credentials/git_credential.go, internal/template/credentials.go and related tests; .gitignore excludes .env, .env.local, *.key, credentials.json
**Default / protected branches**: main (default branch); protection status not queryable via gh for this remote
**CI/CD deploy targets**: None configured — CI references GITHUB_TOKEN secret name only (.github/workflows present)
**Network posture**: None configured
**Host containment**: None configured — assume Claude Code runs on an ordinary developer machine with open internet
**Source control**: The trusted repo (anthnel/devdesk) and its remote entire://aws-eu-central-1.entire.io/anthnel/devdesk only (no additional orgs configured)
**Trusted internal domains**: None configured

print('meta keys', dict(meta))
print('meta values (types/depth only)', dict(metaVals))
EOF

import json, collections, glob, os
root = os.path.expanduser('~/.claude/projects')

ms = collections.Counter(); sysub = collections.Counter(); qs = collections.Counter()

    for raw in open(f, 'rb'):
        o = json.loads(raw)
        t = o.get('type')
        if t == 'assistant' and o.get('quotaLimits'):
            qlcount += 1
            q = o['quotaLimits']
            for k in ('status', 'rateLimitType', 'overageStatus'): enums[(k, q.get(k))] += 1
        if t == 'user' and isinstance(o.get('toolUseResult'), dict):
            r = o['toolUseResult']
            if 'agentId' in r or 'totalTokens' in r or 'usage' in r:
                for k in r: tur[k] += 1
                if isinstance(r.get('usage'), dict):
                    for k in r['usage']: turu[k] += 1
        if t == 'cost-state':
            for k, v in (o.get('modelUsage') or {}).items():
                if isinstance(v, dict):
                    for kk in v: ms[kk] += 1
        if t == 'system': sysub[o.get('subtype')] += 1
        if t == 'api-request': qs[o.get('querySource')] += 1
print('quotaLimits lines', qlcount, dict(enums))
print('toolUseResult (agent) keys', dict(tur))
print('toolUseResult.usage keys', dict(turu))
print('cost-state modelUsage entry keys', dict(ms))
print('system subtypes', dict(sysub))
print('api-request querySource', dict(qs))
EOF

The search turned up mixed information, and I couldn't confirm the official Docker docs for this.

- **Default behavior:** `sbx run claude` mounts your project directory and starts Claude Code, and a guide says everything except project files disappears when the sandbox stops (This mounts your project directory into the container and starts Claude Code with --dangerously-skip-permissions by default. The sandbox is disposable).
- **Conflicting claim on ~/.claude:** One guide says sandboxes don't read user-level config from the host ~/.claude, so global CLAUDE.md, preferences, and MCP configs must be recreated inside (Sandboxes don't pick up user-level configuration from your host ~/.claude directory. Only project-level config in the mounted working directory is available inside the container.).
- **Workaround that mounts ~/.claude:** A DEV Community post describes recreating a sandbox with `sbx create` and adding `~/.claude/` as an extra mount with write access. It also warns that memory kept only inside the container is lost on deletion, and suggests saving it to a host path such as ~/.claude/MEMORY.md (sbx create claude --name shop-dev with the project directory, ~/.m2/repository read-only, and ~/.claude/ with write access; the /memory context is stored inside the container by default, which means it's gone when the container is deleted).
- **Kit-managed volumes:** The official `sbx/claude-mixin` kit declares several volumes for session state, including conversation transcripts and per-session state used by `claude -c` (com.docker.sandbox/volume@1 for conversation transcripts; per-session state JSON, load-bearing for claude -c). The listing doesn't say whether these map to host directories.
- **Stability caveat:** A University of Cambridge guide notes that the sbx env and kit commands are marked experimental and may change (they can change or be removed in any release).

**Bottom line:** Whether ~/.claude persists to the host depends on whether you add it as an extra mount with `sbx create`. Default `sbx run` doesn't clearly do this. I'd check Docker's current sbx documentation before relying on it.

for x in F:

print('MB', round(nbytes/1e6,1), 'python full parse s', round(time.time()-t0,2))

# Agent usage monitor : faisabilité (architect, 2026-10-24)

**Verdict : faisable, sans nouvelle dépendance Go**, à trois conditions : (1) dédupliquer par `message.id` en gardant la **dernière** ligne, (2) lire les fichiers par polling incrémental dans un `Cmd`, l'agrégat n'étant modifié que dans `Update`, (3) S-08 ne démarre qu'après une vérification sur l'hôte qui lance `sbx`.
Légende : [O] observé sur cette machine (structure seulement, aucun contenu lu ni rapporté), [E] estimation.

## Observations locales qui changent le plan

- [O] 7 projets, 130 JSONL (178 Mo), 91 sous-agents. Plus gros fichier : 15 Mo. **Plus longue ligne : 1,27 Mo** : le `bufio.Scanner` par défaut (64 Kio) échoue. Il faut un `bufio.Reader` ou un `Scanner.Buffer` plafonné, et compter les lignes ignorées.
- [O] 19 types de lignes (`assistant`, `user`, `attachment`, `api-request-blob`, `cost-state`, `agent-name`…). Versions 2.1.283 à 2.1.302 seulement : les transcripts plus anciens sont purgés à 30 jours, donc la fixture « autre version » devra être **synthétique**.
- [O] **Dédup mesurée** sur tous les transcripts : la somme naïve gonfle les totaux ×1,9 à ×2,5. Garder la *première* ligne sous-estime `output_tokens` de 2,7 %, ce qui dépasse la tolérance de 2 %. La dernière ligne porte toujours le maximum (2968 groupes sur 2968). Il faut aussi exclure le modèle `<synthetic>`.
- [O] Le transcript parent ne contient aucune ligne `isSidechain` ni `agentId` : aucun double comptage entre fichiers. Le `toolUseResult` de l'outil Agent n'a pas de `usage`, mais il contient `prompt` : à ne jamais décoder.
- [O] `subagents/agent-<id>.meta.json` contient `finished: bool` (87 sur 91 ; absent pour un agent en cours ou une ancienne version) et `spawnDepth` (toujours 1 ici, l'arbre a donc 2 niveaux en pratique). Il contient aussi `description`, un texte de tâche, donc du contenu.
- [O] `~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json` (non documenté) : `sessionId`, `pid`, `status` (`busy` ou `idle`), `updatedAt`. C'est un bon indice pour savoir qu'une session est vivante. Repli : la date de modification du fichier.
- [O] Lignes `cost-state` : `modelUsage` par modèle (`inputTokens`… `costUSD`), écrites par Claude Code lui-même. C'est une **référence possible pour la règle des 2 %**, peut-être meilleure que ccusage.
- [O] Champ `quotaLimits` sur une ligne `assistant` (`status`, `rateLimitType: five_hour`, `resetsAt`). Il n'apparaît qu'au rejet. Cela nuance research.md : signal partiel de quota, à garder pour la v2.
- [O] Python lit les 178 Mo en 0,65 s [E : Go est du même ordre]. Une relecture complète est donc acceptable pour `ctrl+r`, mais jamais dans `Update`.
- [O] Ni `sbx` ni `docker` ne sont installés sur cette machine. Le seul hook configuré est `SessionStart`, il y a une statusline, aucun réglage OTel. Les sessions `sbx` ne sont **pas observables d'ici**.

## 1. Risques techniques (classés)

| # | Risque | P / I | Parade |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Format non contractuel (nouveaux types, champs renommés) | haute / haute | Décoder ligne à ligne dans une struct qui ne porte **que** des champs numériques et des identifiants, ignorer les types inconnus, compteurs `skipped` et `unknownVersion` affichés dans l'en-tête (dégradation visible). Fixtures datées et versionnées. |
| 2 | Dédup | certaine / haute | Clé `message.id` (+ `requestId`), la dernière ligne gagne, carte par session (et non par fichier) : elle couvre un futur parent qui recopierait les lignes des sous-agents. Exclure `<synthetic>`. Fixer en S-01 la référence (ccusage ou `cost-state`) : si ccusage garde la première ligne, l'écart de 2,7 % est structurel. |
| 3 | Lecture incrémentale | moyenne / haute | Un offset par fichier ; une dernière ligne sans `\n` est gardée en reste et relue au tick suivant ; une taille inférieure à l'offset déclenche une relecture complète ; une ligne au-delà du plafond est sautée et comptée. On suppose les fichiers en ajout seul (les `compact_boundary` sont ajoutées, pas réécrites). |
| 4 | Polling ou watcher | moyenne / moyenne | **Polling `tea.Tick` (2 s) + `stat`**, le modèle existant (suivi du viewer, ports, conteneurs). Pas de `fsnotify` : c'est une nouvelle dépendance, peu fiable sur les montages 9p, virtiofs et WSL, précisément ceux de S-08. Ne sonder que la session ouverte et le répertoire `subagents/` (nouveaux agents). Arrêt quand la session est inactive et que tous les `finished` sont à vrai. |
| 5 | Règle 110 / `Update` non bloquant | faible si conçu ainsi / haute | Le `Cmd` reçoit une **copie** des offsets et rend `UsageDeltaMsg{gen, file, from, to, records}`. `Update` n'applique le delta que si `from == offset courant` et `gen` est le dernier, sinon il l'abandonne (même schéma que `toolsGen`). Une seule lecture en vol par session. `mise run test-race` est obligatoire. |
| 6 | Confidentialité | moyenne / haute | Les lignes contiennent prompts, thinking, `wireToolInputs`, `toolUseResult.prompt`. On ne loggue jamais une ligne, et une erreur de décodage ne cite que le fichier et l'offset. On ne compte les blocs `tool_use` que par leur `type`. `description` et `ai-title` ne s'affichent pas (voir Q3). |
| 7 | Intégration au routeur | faible / moyenne | Les tests de contrat attrapent les oublis (`TestEveryViewSuppliesItsHeaderAndHelp`, keymap, `AllViewNames`). Points d'entrée listés en §3. |
| 8 | Entrée non fiable (S-08) | moyenne / moyenne | Un sandbox écrit ces fichiers : plafond de ligne, pas de suivi des liens symboliques hors des racines, pas de décodage de chemin depuis le nom de répertoire (lire `cwd`). |
| 9 | Portabilité | faible / moyenne | `~/.claude` vient de `os.UserHomeDir`, et `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` est honoré s'il est défini (Windows inclus). |

## 2. Effort par story

| Story | Effort | Hypothèse qui le justifie |
|---|---|---|
| S-01 spike | **S** (½ à 1 j) | Ce document en a fait une partie (structure, dédup, `meta.json`). Reste à faire : lancer ccusage sur 3 sessions et noter sa règle de dédup, vérifier `sbx` **sur l'hôte qui le lance**, créer la fixture synthétique « autre version ». |
| S-02 parseur | **M** | Package pur sans TUI ; struct à champs numériques ; dédup ; tolérance ; 5 à 8 fixtures. Le critère des 2 % dépend de la référence choisie en S-01. |
| S-03 liste + arbre | **M**, découpage conseillé | C'est la première vue : enregistrement complet (§3). **S-03a** liste des sessions (projet = `cwd`, date = mtime, triées) : S. **S-03b** `→` vers la table des agents (orchestrateur puis sous-agents, rôle, modèle, tokens) sur le modèle runs → targets de `:jobs` : S. |
| S-04 tri + part | **S** | `.` et `Less` sont fournis par `datatable`. Colonne `%` en `SizingFixed` ; le dernier arrondi est absorbé par la ligne principale pour que la somme fasse 100. Distinguer deux agents du même rôle se fait par l'`agentId` court. |
| S-05 direct | **L**, à redécouper | **S-05a** lecteur incrémental dans le package (offsets, reste de ligne, troncature, plafond), sans TUI : M. **S-05b** polling dans la vue (tick, `gen`, découverte des nouveaux agents, arrêt sur session terminée, `ctrl+r` = relecture complète) : M. |
| S-06 état / activité | **M** | État = `finished`, sinon « en cours » si la session est vivante, sinon « inconnu ». Inactif = aucune ligne depuis plus de 5 min. Compter les `tool_use` par `(message.id, apiBlockIndex)`, car les lignes streamées répètent le message. Durée = premier → dernier `timestamp`. |
| S-07 coût indicatif | **M** | Nouvelle section de configuration (`agent_usage.prices` par modèle, avec les tarifs distincts cache 5 min / 1 h / lecture), `-` si le tarif est inconnu. C'est une carte, pas un scalaire : la vue `:cfg` ne l'édite pas, l'édition passe par le YAML (Q4). |
| S-08 sandbox | **S** (option A) à **L** (option B) | Avec l'option A, DevDesk n'ajoute que des racines de transcripts multiples et une colonne « Source » ; le reste est une procédure `sbx` documentée. À réécrire après S-01. |

## 3. Packages et intégration

- `internal/agentusage` (pur, sans Bubble Tea) : `Discover(roots) []SessionRef`, `type Reader` (offsets et reste, valeur copiable), `ReadDelta(ref, offsets) (Delta, error)`, `type Aggregate` avec `Apply(Delta) Aggregate` (dédup, totaux par agent), `Liveness(ref)` (`sessions/*.json` + mtime). `internal/agentusage/pricing` arrivera avec S-07.
- `internal/ui/agentusage` : `Model` (deux niveaux `datatable`, fil d'Ariane sous la table, Règle 123), `availability.go` (Règle 130), `GetHelpContent` (Règle 114), les 4 méthodes de `HeaderView` (compteur de sessions et d'agents dans `GetHeaderInfo`), et l'état de chargement dans le pied de page (Règles 128 et 139).
- Points d'entrée : `internal/command/parser.go` (`ViewAgentUsage`, table `viewNames`), `internal/app/command_line.go` (`createView`), `docs/architecture/` (nouveau fichier, et une ligne dans le tableau de `.claude/CLAUDE.md`).
- **Commande** : `:usage` / `:us` (Hypothèse : `ag`, `us` et `u` sont libres, à arbitrer en Q1).
- **Clavier : aucune lettre d'action en MVP.** `→`/`enter` descend, `←`/`esc` remonte, `.` trie, `/` filtre, `ctrl+r` relit. Les lettres libres (`Q`, `Z`) ne sont pas consommées. Un éventuel filtre « actives seulement » serait une minuscule déclarée dans `keymap.localToggles`. Plus tard : `Y` (copier l'id de session), déjà dans le vocabulaire.
- Pas de `jobs.Run` : le polling n'est pas un travail lancé par l'utilisateur. On ne l'inscrit au registre que si l'on veut voir la relecture complète dans `:jobs`, ce qui n'est pas nécessaire.

## 4. Sandbox `sbx` : transport

D'après des sources tierces, les transcripts d'un `sbx` vivent dans un **volume géré par le kit** et ne sont pas sur l'hôte ; `sbx create` accepte des montages supplémentaires ([sbx/claude-mixin](https://hub.docker.com/r/sbx/claude-mixin), [DEV Community](https://dev.to/thr0n/claude-code-in-docker-sandboxes-239g)). Non vérifié : `sbx` est absent de cette machine.

| Option | Avantages | Risques |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Monter un répertoire hôte dédié** (`~/.devdesk/agent-usage/sbx/<nom>`) comme `~/.claude/projects` du sandbox ; DevDesk le déclare comme racine supplémentaire | Aucun code de transport ; même parseur ; quasi temps réel ; survit à la suppression du sandbox | Il faut recréer le sandbox (`sbx create`) ; le sandbox écrit sur l'hôte. **Ne jamais monter tout `~/.claude`** : le sandbox pourrait écrire `settings.json`/hooks exécutés par l'hôte (évasion). Montages 9p/virtiofs : d'où le polling. |
| B. Lire le volume via `sbx exec … tail -c +offset` | Rien à reconfigurer côté sandbox | CLI expérimentale, un processus par tick, latence, dépend de l'auth `sbx` ; effort L |
| C. Hook dans le sandbox (`Stop`, `SubagentStop`) qui copie le transcript dans le dépôt monté (`.worktrees/…`) | Utilise le montage existant | Les hooks ne portent pas de tokens (il faut copier le fichier), écrit dans l'arbre du dépôt (gitignore), installe une config dans chaque sandbox, latence par événement |
| D. OTel : le sandbox exporte en OTLP vers un récepteur DevDesk | Attribution officielle (`agent_id` sur les événements) | Hors MVP (brief), récepteur à embarquer, sortie réseau du sandbox vers l'hôte via le proxy `sbx`, 5 s/60 s, variables d'environnement par session |

**Recommandation : A**, avec un montage **dédié et limité aux transcripts**, sous réserve que S-01 confirme sur l'hôte `sbx` que (a) le montage peut remplacer `~/.claude/projects` sans casser `claude -c`, et (b) les fichiers sont visibles et ajoutés au fil de l'eau côté hôte. Sinon, se replier sur C.

## 5. Ordre de livraison

1. S-01 (Go / no-go, dédup de référence, constat `sbx`).
2. S-02 puis S-05a (même package, en TDD, sans TUI ; parallélisable une fois l'API `Delta`/`Aggregate` figée).
3. S-03a, puis S-03b et S-04 (S-04 parallélisable avec S-03b).
4. S-05b (critère de succès « en direct < 3 s »).
5. S-06, puis S-07 (indépendante, peut glisser), puis S-08 selon S-01.

## Questions ouvertes (pour l'utilisateur)

1. **Nom de la commande** : `:usage`/`:us` (recommandé), `:agents`/`:ag`, ou `:agent-usage`/`:au` ?
2. **Référence des 2 %** : ccusage (externe, règle de dédup à vérifier) ou les lignes `cost-state` de Claude Code (interne, par modèle et non par agent) ? Recommandation : `cost-state` pour le total de session, ccusage en contrôle secondaire.
3. **Afficher `meta.description` / `ai-title`** pour distinguer les agents et nommer les sessions ? Ce sont des textes de tâche, contraires à « jamais de contenu ». Recommandation : non en MVP (agent = rôle + `agentId` court, session = projet + date).
4. **Tarifs (S-07)** : édition YAML seule acceptable, ou faut-il un éditeur dans `:cfg` (ce qui ajoute M) ?
5. **Où tourne `sbx`** : sur l'hôte Windows évoqué dans `.claude/CLAUDE.md` ? DevDesk lit-il alors des chemins Windows (`%USERPROFILE%\.claude`) ? Cela conditionne S-01 et S-08.
6. **Recréer les sandboxes** avec un montage supplémentaire (option A) : acceptable ?
